subtitle: Examine how rules, defaults and resources in public programs can contribute to unequal results by race, and lead an evidence-based review with clear decision authority and follow-up.
audience: For DHS and DSD leaders, managers, policy and program staff, and facilitators who review policies, design processes or guide team conversations about fair access and civil rights.

lessons.title: Intent and effect: two questions about the same rule
objectives: Distinguish a question about intent from a question about effect when a concern about fairness is raised.
Explain why a rule can produce unequal results by race without anyone intending harm.
Route a concern about one person's conduct to the person or area responsible, and keep patterns in results with the team that owns the process.
Write an intent question and an effect question about the same rule.
lessons.teaching:
Conversations about race and public programs often stall because people are answering different questions. One person hears a question about character: did someone mean to treat people differently? Another person is describing a pattern in results that no single person created. Both questions matter. They call for different responses, so it helps to name which one is on the table before choosing what to do.

The intent question asks whether anyone treated a person differently because of race, color, national origin, disability or another protected trait. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in programs that receive federal funds. The Minnesota Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination in public services and in employment. A concern about one employee's conduct is serious. It goes to the person or area responsible, such as the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division or Human Resources, which make formal determinations.

The effect question asks how a rule, default or resource works in practice for the people who must use it. A deadline, a mailing process, an English-only form or a weekday-only phone line can produce different results for different households, even when every employee applies it the same way. Race Forward distinguishes institutional racism within an organization from structural racism across connected institutions and historical systems. These concepts direct attention beyond individual motives. A difference in outcomes is a reason to investigate; it does not by itself establish its cause or a legal violation.

Depending on their roles, DHS and DSD staff may help shape procedures, notices, service hours, data collection or contracts. Each change must stay within delegated authority, legal requirements and required deadlines. Training one employee cannot fix a procedure that produces unequal results no matter who carries it out. An authorized change may address the barrier, but its effects still need to be evaluated. When results differ and no one can point to a biased act, the useful next question is which factors may contribute, what evidence could distinguish them, and who can authorize a response. Conduct and process concerns may overlap. Refer possible discrimination promptly through established channels while examining the process; do not wait for proof of intent or treat a team review as a substitute for required reporting.
lessons.keyPoint: Distinguish questions about intent and effect while recognizing that they can overlap. Refer possible discrimination promptly, examine process evidence, and test which changes may address the identified barrier.
lessons.example: Practice case: In a DSD program team meeting, Marisol shares that families of color on the team's waiting list are less likely than white families to return a required follow-up form by the deadline. Dennis responds that the form is the same for everyone and staff treat all families the same. Priya, the supervisor, notices that Dennis is answering an intent question about staff conduct. Marisol is raising an effect question about how a deadline, a mailing process and an English-only form work for different households.
lessons.question: What should Priya do next?
choices: Ask the team to review their own interactions with families for signs of personal bias before looking at anything else.
Name the two questions, thank both colleagues, and propose mapping how the form, deadline and mailing process work for different households.
Close the topic, since no one has identified a discriminatory act and the form treats everyone identically.
feedback: Starting here treats a possible process pattern as a question about personal character. Staff may become defensive, and the form and the deadline stay unexamined.
This separates the two questions without dismissing either one. It moves the team toward the parts of the process that could be producing the pattern, which the team has the authority to examine.
Identical treatment does not establish equal results. Closing the topic leaves a pattern unexamined even though the team owns the process that may be producing it.
lessons.reflection: Think of a work conversation about fairness where people seemed to talk past each other, or use the practice case above. Privately note which question each person was answering, intent or effect, and how naming the two might have changed the conversation.
lessons.action: Choose one routine process your team owns, such as a notice, a deadline or an intake step. Write two questions about it: an intent question (did anyone mean to treat people differently?) and an effect question (does it work equally well for people in different circumstances?). Bring the effect question to your next team meeting.

check.question: Which of these is an effect question about a rule?
check.correct: Does this rule work equally well for the people in different circumstances who must meet it?
wrong: Did the employee who applied the rule mean to treat someone differently?
Was the rule written without any mention of race?
check.feedback: An effect question looks at how a rule performs for the people who must meet it. Whether someone meant to treat a person differently is a separate question about conduct. Neutral wording describes the text of a rule, not its results.

lessons.title: How neutral rules land on unequal histories
objectives: Describe documented Minnesota history, such as racial covenants and redlining, that shaped present-day conditions.
Explain how a rule written the same for everyone can produce different results because of the conditions it meets.
Identify common DHS process features that may carry historical disadvantage forward.
Find out whether a requirement comes from law, rule, policy, contract or habit, and who owns it.
lessons.teaching:
A neutral rule is written without reference to race. That describes its wording, not whether it is justified, accessible or lawful. Examine how it works for the people affected and what explains any differences. A rule meets people who arrive with different amounts of wealth, time, trust, transportation, documentation and prior experience with government. Historical policies can shape those conditions, alongside other influences that require examination.

Minnesota has a well-documented example. The University of Minnesota Libraries' Mapping Prejudice project has identified thousands of racial covenants in Minneapolis and Hennepin County. These were clauses written into property deeds to keep people who were not white from buying or living on the land. The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis has described how covenants, federal redlining maps that marked neighborhoods of color as high risk, and federal mortgage insurance practices that largely excluded buyers of color combined to shape who could buy homes and build wealth. It also describes the freeway built through Saint Paul's Rondo neighborhood, a center of Black community life. In its 2021 article, the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis reported that Minnesota's gap between white homeownership and homeownership among households of color and Native American households was among the largest in the nation at that time. Minnesota Compass publishes current homeownership rates by race. Use the published numbers and their date rather than repeating a figure from memory.

Housing wealth and stability can affect a family’s resources for care, transport and responding to public agencies. Historical exclusion therefore provides context for examining present barriers. It does not tell you a particular household’s resources, trust or preferences. For example, ask whether a mailing rule reaches people with changing addresses and whether the records support that explanation. Asset rules vary by program and may exclude certain property; do not infer eligibility or hardship from race or homeownership.

For DHS and DSD work, the practical skill is to look at a rule and ask what it assumes about the person on the other side. Documentation requirements assume access to records. Mailed notices with short deadlines assume stable housing. English-only phone lines assume a language. A degree requirement for a position assumes one path through education. Some requirements are necessary and set by law; others are habits. Separating the two is work that leaders and program staff can do, and approved alternatives should follow clear standards. Individual accommodations and other lawful exceptions may also be required; identical treatment is not the only way to provide fair access.
lessons.keyPoint: A rule can be neutral on paper and unequal in effect, because it lands on conditions shaped by history. Ask what each requirement assumes about the person who has to meet it.
lessons.example: Practice case: Tomas manages a unit that verifies information for a disability services program. The unit requires three months of paper bank statements. Staff report that some applicants repeatedly miss the deadline. When Tomas asks the team what the requirement assumes, they list a bank account, mail at a stable address, and the ability to visit a branch or print statements. Kiana, a newer analyst, asks whether the program rule actually requires paper statements or whether other verification is allowed.
lessons.question: What should Tomas do with Kiana's question?
choices: Check with the policy owner what the rule actually requires, list acceptable alternatives if any exist, and look at who is missing the deadline.
Keep the current practice because changing it could look like lowering the standard for some applicants.
Allow staff to waive the requirement for anyone who seems to be struggling.
feedback: This separates the legal requirement from the unit's habit, keeps the verification standard the same for everyone, and brings evidence to the question instead of guessing.
Keeping a habit that is not required is not the same as protecting a standard. The verification goal can stay the same while the accepted ways of meeting it change for every applicant.
Waivers based on impressions are applied unevenly, may go beyond staff authority, and can create new unfairness. The fix belongs at the level of the rule and the policy owner.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider one requirement in your own work that feels ordinary to you, or use the bank statement requirement in the practice case. What does it assume about the people who must meet it, and how confident are you that the assumption holds for everyone?
lessons.action: Pick one requirement in a form, notice or process you touch. Write down what it assumes about the person (address, time, language, records, transportation, trust). Then find out whether the requirement comes from law, rule, policy, contract or habit, and note who owns it.

check.question: What does it mean to say a rule is neutral but its results are not?
check.correct: The rule does not mention race, yet it works less well for some groups because of the conditions and histories it meets.
wrong: The rule was secretly written to exclude a group.
The rule is fair because everyone is treated identically, so any difference must come from individual choices.
check.feedback: Neutral wording describes the text of a rule. Neutral results describe how it performs. Looking at the gap between the two does not assume hidden intent, and it does not assume that different results reflect only personal choices.

lessons.title: Title VI, disparate impact and reading data responsibly
objectives: Use three design questions (effect, justification, alternatives) and explain how federal Title VI rules on disparate impact changed in 2025 and 2026.
Identify the limits of public data on differences by race before using it to support a conclusion.
Distinguish an internal program review from a formal legal determination.
Plan how to combine data with the account of people affected.
lessons.teaching:
Disparate impact is a legal idea leaders should understand at a working level, including how it changed. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in programs that receive federal funds. For decades, federal Title VI regulations also reached criteria or methods of administration with discriminatory effects. The United States Department of Justice removed those provisions effective December 10, 2025. The United States Department of Health and Human Services, which funds DHS, removed its parallel provisions effective July 24, 2026. The cited final rules state that Title VI prohibits only intentional discrimination and that they will not pursue disparate-impact liability. Both also say data on unequal outcomes can still help prove intentional discrimination. Whether other federal or Minnesota law reaches a given practice is a question for legal counsel.

The earlier analysis asked three questions. First, is there an adverse effect: does a specific policy cause a harm that falls disproportionately on one group? Second, is there a substantial legitimate justification: is the policy necessary to meet an important goal, supported by evidence rather than speculation? Third, is there a less discriminatory alternative that would meet the same goal for everyone?

These three questions are presented here as a historical framework and a design exercise, not a current legal test. Confirm applicable law and any relevant court orders with legal counsel before acting. You can still use them as a design discipline, because a careful program team asks them anyway: What is the effect? Why is this needed? Is there another way? What you should not do is announce a legal conclusion. Whether a practice violates Title VI, the Minnesota Human Rights Act or any other law is a formal determination for legal counsel, the Equal Opportunity and Access Division, or an enforcement agency. Your job in a program review is to surface the pattern, document the reasoning and route concerns to the person or area responsible.

Data is where many reviews go wrong. Public sources such as Minnesota Compass, Minnesota Department of Health reports and DHS program dashboards can show differences by race and ethnicity. They cannot, on their own, tell you why a difference exists. Before using a number, check its date, its definitions, which groups were combined, how small the counts are, and whether data is missing more often for some groups. A combined category can hide large differences between, for example, Somali, Hmong, Karen and Ethiopian Minnesotans. Small numbers can swing sharply from year to year. Do not invent a figure or present an unsupported estimate as fact. Published estimates may be appropriate when their method, uncertainty and source are clear. Protect small groups from identification and use approved disclosure controls.

Numbers describe patterns; people describe how the pattern is lived. The Equity Analysis Toolkit pairs data and evidence with engagement for this reason. Talk with the people and partners affected, including counties and Tribal Nations where they administer services, about what the process is like from their side. Their accounts can suggest explanations to investigate, but do not alone establish causation. Work with Tribal Nations through the applicable government-to-government process rather than treating consultation as an ordinary stakeholder meeting.
lessons.keyPoint: Use the three questions as a design discipline (effect, justification, alternatives), know that federal Title VI rules changed in 2025 and 2026, read data with its limits in view, and leave legal conclusions to the people or areas that make them.
lessons.example: Practice case: Grace, a data analyst, finds that denials for a service authorization are more common in two racial groups. Her manager, Olu, is drafting a briefing for leadership. A colleague suggests titling the briefing 'Evidence of discrimination in authorizations.' Grace notes that the counts for one group are small, that race is missing for many records, and that the team has not yet looked at which denial reasons drive the pattern.
lessons.question: How should Olu frame the briefing?
choices: Title it as evidence of discrimination, because naming the problem strongly is the best way to get leadership attention.
Leave out the pattern until the data is perfect, to avoid alarming anyone.
Describe the pattern and its data limits, list the next steps for analysis, and note that any legal question will be referred to legal counsel and the Equal Opportunity and Access Division.
feedback: The briefing would state a legal conclusion the team cannot make and the data cannot yet support. That can undermine trust in a pattern that may be real.
Data is rarely perfect. Withholding a credible pattern delays examination and can leave a harmful process in place.
This reports what is known, is honest about the limits, proposes how to learn more and routes formal questions to the people and areas that decide them.
lessons.reflection: Think about a time a number describing differences between groups was used at work, or use the briefing in the practice case. Privately note whether its date, definitions or data gaps were mentioned, and what would help you ask about those limits comfortably.
lessons.action: Find one published Minnesota figure that shows a difference between groups in your area, from Minnesota Compass, the Minnesota Department of Health or a DHS report. Write down its source, date, definitions, which groups are combined and one thing it cannot tell you. Share the note with a colleague who uses the same data.

check.question: In the three design questions from this lesson, what is the third question?
check.correct: Whether a less discriminatory alternative exists that would meet the same legitimate goal.
wrong: Whether the staff who applied the policy intended to discriminate.
Whether the affected group is larger than a set percentage of the population.
check.feedback: The questions ask about adverse effect, then substantial legitimate justification, then less discriminatory alternatives. Intent is what the Department of Justice and the Department of Health and Human Services Title VI rules now turn on, but it is not one of these design questions, and there is no single population threshold. A justified policy can still be a problem if a less harmful alternative would meet the same goal.

lessons.title: Reviewing a policy with the Equity Analysis Toolkit
objectives: Apply the State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit questions to a practice DHS policy.
Identify who holds decision rights over a rule, default or resource under review.
Explain how workplace habits can operate as unexamined defaults without accusing anyone.
Plan a change with an owner, a date to look again and a way to report back to the people affected.
lessons.teaching:
The State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit gives agencies a structured way to examine who a decision affects. Its quick guide works through impact assessment, partner engagement, data and evidence, access and accessibility, monitoring and evaluation, resources, and implementation and accountability. Its core questions are plain. What outcomes do we intend? Who are we including? How can we collaborate? What impact will result? How will we be accountable? How will we communicate?

The toolkit is only as strong as the map of authority you bring to it. Institutions repeat what they do not examine, and defaults last because they work for the people who set them. So for each part of a policy, ask who decided it, who can change it and who bears the cost if it stays. Some features are set by federal or state law. Others are set by DHS policy, by a division, by a contract, or by a supervisor's habit. Mapping decision rights keeps a review from ending in recommendations that no one has the authority to act on.

Habits deserve the same attention as rules. Ideas about what counts as professional communication, a reasonable pace, credible evidence or appropriate expertise often reflect the habits of the people who set the rule. Those habits get presented as a universal standard, and the mainstream default becomes the rule everyone is measured against. Naming this is a design observation, not an accusation. If a hiring panel treats one communication style as a sign of competence, review the selection methods with HR and use approved, job-related criteria with appropriate accommodations. If a stakeholder meeting assumes everyone can attend on a weekday afternoon, ask participants whether another time, accessible format or written option would remove the barrier; one alternative may not meet every need.

Finally, connect the analysis to a decision with an owner. A completed review records a supported decision: retain the practice, revise it, test an authorized alternative, or seek further review. Explain why, identify who can act, and set a follow-up date. Tell participants what was decided and what remains unresolved. The toolkit stresses action and continued reassessment. Monitor benefits and unintended harms after a change. A newly discovered barrier calls for a response; it is not automatically evidence of success.
lessons.keyPoint: A policy review needs a reasoned decision, an accountable owner, a follow-up date and a report back to participants. Evidence may support retaining a practice, revising it or seeking further review.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD policy team is revising how people request a change in their service plan. Current practice requires a request by phone during business hours. Hye-jin leads a review using the Equity Analysis Toolkit. Conversations with self-advocates and two county case managers show that people who work hourly jobs or rely on interpreters struggle to reach staff. The team drafts a written and online request option. Ahmed points out that the phone-only practice is set by a division procedure, not by law.
lessons.question: What should Hye-jin do next?
choices: Publish the analysis as a report and let division leaders decide later whether to act on it.
Take the draft change to the procedure owner with the analysis, propose a start date and a review date, and plan how to tell participants what changed.
Pause until the team can prove the phone-only practice caused worse outcomes for specific racial groups.
feedback: A report without an owner or a decision point is how reviews stall. The team already knows who controls the procedure.
This uses the decision-rights map, connects the analysis to a concrete change that applies to everyone, sets a time to look again and closes the loop with the people who contributed.

Evidence matters, but the team already has credible accounts of a barrier within its own authority to fix. Waiting for proof about one group can leave an avoidable barrier in place for everyone it affects.
lessons.reflection: Consider a workplace habit you rely on, such as a meeting format, a writing style or a way of showing expertise, or use the phone-only practice in the practice case. Privately, who does it work well for, and who might it quietly screen out?
lessons.action: Use the job aid to map authority for one policy or practice your team owns. Identify its legal or policy basis, the evidence about its effects, and who can decide what happens next. Propose retaining it, testing an authorized change or seeking further review, with reasons and a follow-up date.

check.question: Why does a policy review map decision rights?
check.correct: So recommendations go to the person or group that actually has authority to change the rule, default or resource.
wrong: So the team can assign blame to the person who created the original rule.
So features set by law can be left out of the analysis.
check.feedback: Mapping decision rights moves a review from analysis to action. It is not a blame exercise. Features set by law still matter; they may call for a legislative proposal, guidance or a way to reduce the burden rather than a local change.

cards.back: Did anyone treat a person differently because of race, color, national origin, disability or another protected trait? Concerns about conduct go to the person or area responsible.
How does this rule, default or resource work in practice for the people in different circumstances who must meet it?
A rule written the same for everyone that performs differently because of the conditions and histories it meets.

A policy neutral on its face that causes a harm falling disproportionately on a protected group. As of July 24, 2026, Department of Justice and Department of Health and Human Services Title VI regulations no longer impose liability on this basis. The questions about effect, justification and alternatives remain useful for design.
Who set a feature of a policy, who can change it, and whether it comes from law, rule, policy, contract or habit.

aid.heading: Separate intent and effect
items: Ask about both conduct and process; concerns may overlap and required reporting must not wait for a team review.
Route alleged discriminatory conduct to the Equal Opportunity and Access Division and Human Resources; do not investigate it yourself.
For patterns in results, ask which rule, default or resource could be producing them.

aid.heading: Examine the rule
items: Write what the requirement assumes about the person who must meet it.
Find whether it comes from law, rule, policy, contract or habit, and who owns it.
Ask the three design questions: effect, justification, alternative.
Use approved standards and alternatives, including individual accommodations or other lawful exceptions when needed.
Leave legal conclusions to legal counsel and the Equal Opportunity and Access Division.

aid.heading: Use data carefully
items: Cite each figure and date; label estimates and their uncertainty rather than presenting unsupported numbers as facts.
Check definitions, denominators, combined groups, small counts, missing data and privacy protections.
Pair data with participants’ accounts; use the applicable government-to-government process when working with Tribal Nations.

aid.heading: Close the loop
items: Record the supported decision: retain, revise, test an authorized option or seek further review.
Name an owner, a start date and a date to look again.
Tell the people who informed the review what changed and what did not.
Treat a newly discovered barrier as the next question, not a failure.

sources.title: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, United States Code title 42, section 2000d (Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School)
sources.note: Supports the statement that Title VI prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in programs that receive federal funds (lessons 1 and 3).

sources.title: Minnesota Human Rights Act, chapter 363A
sources.note: Supports the statement that Minnesota law prohibits discrimination in public services and employment (lessons 1 and 3).

sources.title: United States Department of Justice — Rescinding Portions of Department of Justice Title VI Regulations, Federal Register volume 90, page 57141 (effective December 10, 2025)
sources.note: Removes the disparate-impact provisions from Department of Justice Title VI regulations. States that data on unequal outcomes can still help prove intentional discrimination (lesson 3).

sources.title: United States Department of Health and Human Services — Rescinding Portions of the Department of Health and Human Services Title VI Regulations, Federal Register document 2026-15000 (effective July 24, 2026)
sources.note: Removes the parallel provisions, including title 45 of the Code of Federal Regulations, section 80.3(b)(2). The department funds DHS. Formal determinations about its effect belong to legal counsel and enforcement agencies (lesson 3).

sources.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis — Systemic racism haunts homeownership rates in Minnesota (2021)
sources.note: Supports the history of covenants, redlining, federal mortgage practices and the Rondo freeway, and the finding that Minnesota's homeownership gap ranks among the largest nationally. The ranking reflects the article's date (lesson 2).

sources.title: University of Minnesota Libraries — Mapping Prejudice
sources.note: Supports the definition of racial covenants and the project's documentation of covenants in Minneapolis and Hennepin County (lesson 2).

sources.title: Minnesota Compass — Housing (homeownership rate by race)
sources.note: Public source of current Minnesota homeownership rates by race. The course points learners to it rather than quoting figures; check the date of any number used (lessons 2 and 3).

sources.title: State of Minnesota — Equity Analysis Toolkit: A Quick Guide
sources.note: Supports the toolkit criteria and core questions in lessons 3 and 4. The toolkit is now also presented at mn.gov/oeoa/resources/equity-analysis-toolkit.

sources.title: Race Forward — What is Racial Equity?
sources.note: Cited only as an example of an organization that uses the terms institutional and structural racism for patterns in systems (lesson 1). The course explains the terms in plain words rather than teaching from this framework.

sources.title: Current 45 CFR 80.3 — Discrimination prohibited
sources.note: Current HHS regulation checked November 16, 2026. Read with the cited final rule; legal counsel must assess applicability and relevant court orders.

sources.title: Current 28 CFR 42.104 — Discrimination prohibited
sources.note: Current DOJ Title VI regulation accompanies the December 2025 final rule. Department-specific changes are not presented as repeal of other civil-rights laws.
